DILG BAGONG Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA cor. Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City www.dilq_gov.ph DILG OPINION NO. S. MAY 19 2025 RUPERTO BUSCATO lifeaidphil@yahoo.com Dear Mr. Buscato. This refers to your electronic mail dated 25 February 2025, received by this Department on 26 February 2025, in which you raised the query: "Is it legal to display the faces of elected officials and the Barangay Secretary and Treasurer on the official uniform of barangay employees?" After careful evaluation, please be advised that, aside from the civil service rules on the proper dress code for government officials and employees as set forth in Memorandum Circular No. 16, series of 2024, there are currently no specific laws or regulations governing the design of government uniforms. Furthermore, there is no existing statute explicitly prohibiting the use of images of barangay officials on the official uniforms of barangay personnel. Nevertheless, we find relevant the Department's Memorandum Circular No. 2010-101 , which prohibits the display of names, initials, and/or images of government officials on billboards, signages, and government properties. This circular explicitly mandates that government projects and properties must only contain the official seal or name of the local government unit, in order to prevent the misuse of government resources for personal or political gain. It is also noteworthy that Section 82 of the General Appropriations Act (GAA) of 2021, commonly referred to as the "anti-epal" provision, prohibits the use of names, images, logos, or any identifiable visual representation of public officials on projects funded by the government. Although this provision primarily applies to infrastructure and related government projects, the underlying principle of preventing self-promotion using public funds is similarly applicable when considering the design of official uniforms. While official uniforms of government personnel, including those of barangay employees, are not considered public properties per se, it is prudent to view the practice of displaying images of public officials on uniforms in light of the policy enshrined in both Memorandum Circular No. 2010-101 and the GAA's anti-epal provision. The intent behind the prohibition is to safeguard government resources from being used to promote individual politicians rather than public service. Hence, while there may be no categorical prohibition, the use of public officials' images on official uniforms, especially if government-funded, could be perceived as analogous to putting "Matino, Mahusay at Maaasahan" Trunkline No. (02) 8876 3454

their names or images on government signages, and may be construed as promoting the official rather than the local government unit (LGU) itself. Moreover, considering the constitutional principle that public office is a public trust and the mandate to promote transparency and accountability, it would be prudent for barangay officials to exercise caution in the design of official uniforms to avoid potential perceptions of self-promotion or the misuse of public funds. This opinion is rendered without prejudice to any contrary interpretation that may be issued by competent authorities or the judiciary. We hope this response sufficiently addresses your query. Respectfully, BY THE AUTHORITY OF THE SECRETARY: ATTY. ROMEO P. BENITEZ Undersecretary for External, Legal and Legislative Affairs Page 2 of 2
